\section[\texorpdfstring{\te{శనగలు} (śanagalu)}{శనగలు (śanagalu)}]{\te{శనగలు} (śanagalu) — chickpeas}

\label{lesson:TE-C299-sanagalu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Telugu for hollow, then the Telugu for dim.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{శనగలు}}
\textbf{\te{శనగలు}} — \emph{śanagalu} — \textquotedblleft{}chickpeas\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{శనగలు}} (\emph{śanagalu}) matches Sanskrit \emph{caṇaka}, \textquotedblleft{}chickpea\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 4579), with the Telugu plural ending \emph{-lu}.
\end{cousinweb}

Before the new one: say the Telugu for chickpeas, then the Telugu for mustard seeds.

\textbf{\te{కొత్తిమీర}} — \emph{kottimīra} — \textquotedblleft{}coriander leaves\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{కొత్తిమీర}} (\emph{kottimīra}) probably comes from the northern coriander word, Hindi \emph{kothmīr}, Oriya \emph{kothimiri}, which CDIAL 3380 traces to Sanskrit \emph{kustumbarī}, \textquotedblleft{}coriander\textquotedblright{}; CDIAL calls that word non-Aryan.
\end{cousinweb}
